title: RBAC & Service Accounts
intro: Every pod runs as a ServiceAccount, and RBAC rules decide what that identity — or a real user — is allowed to do. Let's check permissions instead of guessing from error messages.

steps.prompt: List the ServiceAccounts in the namespace.
steps.explanation: If you never specify one, a pod runs as 'default' — which usually has minimal permissions, and that's intentional.
steps.why: Creating a dedicated ServiceAccount per app (like 'ci-bot' here) instead of using 'default' everywhere is what makes RBAC actually meaningful — you can grant each one only what it needs.

steps.prompt: Check what a Role named 'pod-reader' actually allows.
steps.fake_output:
Name: pod-reader
PolicyRule:
  Resources: pods
  Verbs: get, list, watch
steps.explanation: A Role defines permissions (verbs on resources) but grants nothing by itself — it has to be attached to someone via a RoleBinding.
steps.why: A Role is namespace-scoped; if you needed the same permissions across every namespace you'd use a ClusterRole instead.

steps.prompt: See which RoleBinding grants 'pod-reader' to the 'ci-bot' ServiceAccount.
steps.explanation: The Role defines WHAT is allowed; the RoleBinding defines WHO gets it. You need both, and they're separate objects on purpose so one Role can be reused across many bindings.
steps.why: 'kubectl describe rolebinding ci-bot-binding' shows the exact subject (ci-bot) and role it connects — plain 'get' just confirms the binding exists.

steps.prompt: Instead of reading all that, just directly ask: can the 'ci-bot' ServiceAccount create pods?
steps.explanation: 'auth can-i' actually evaluates the RBAC rules for you instead of you manually tracing Role → RoleBinding → verbs by hand.
steps.why: This is almost always faster than the manual describe-role / describe-rolebinding trail above — reach for 'auth can-i' first when the real question is just 'is X allowed to do Y'.
